name: English Violet
lede: English Violet is a dark, bluish purple catalogued by Robert Ridgway in 1912 and again by Maerz and Paul, whose records disagree on when the name itself first appeared.

sections.title: Two dictionaries, two dates
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature places this hue on plate XI, hue 61, tone m, and the ISCC-NBS system later classified it as a dark purple, about 2.1 units from that block's reference color [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists the name too, but our sources carry two different first-recorded dates for it, 1912 and 1928, and nothing in the record resolves which is right [1]. Wikipedia's entry for this color cites the ISCC-NBS classification rather than offering a naming story, so whether "English" points to a dye, a garden flower, or simply a convention of English-language dictionaries is undocumented here [1].

In Munsell terms the chip reads 6.3P 2.9/4.4, dark and moderately saturated [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[auricula-purple]] and [[madder-violet]], at 2.7 and 3.8 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to this color in 21 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.09 percent, and in 10 by the stricter within-painting measure, which makes it rarer than 68 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Inside those paintings it most often sits as a shadow, 50 percent of the 10 [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1800s, at 1.2 times the expected rate [3].

The earliest match in our archive dates to 1545, in a painting attributed to Bronzino, with the latest from 1915, 14 dated paintings in all, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. That earliest match is 367 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, 1912 [2][3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
